questions.q: I bought ___ apples at the market this morning.
questions.why: Use 'some' in affirmative sentences with plural countable nouns.

questions.q: Do you have ___ questions about the lesson?
questions.why: Use 'any' in questions and negatives with plural or uncountable nouns.

questions.q: There isn't ___ milk left in the fridge.
questions.why: Use 'any' in negative sentences for both countable and uncountable nouns.

questions.q: Would you like ___ coffee?
questions.why: Use 'some' in offers and requests even though they are questions.

questions.q: How ___ money do you have with you?
questions.why: Use 'much' with uncountable nouns like 'money'.

questions.q: How ___ people came to the party?
questions.why: Use 'many' with plural countable nouns like 'people'.

questions.q: There is too ___ traffic on the roads today.
questions.why: 'Traffic' is uncountable, so use 'much'.

questions.q: She doesn't have ___ friends in this city.
questions.why: Use 'many' with countable nouns; 'friends' is countable.

questions.q: I have ___ friends who can help us move.
questions.why: Use 'a few' with countable nouns to mean a small but positive number.

questions.q: There is ___ water left, so we can still make tea.
questions.why: Use 'a little' with uncountable nouns to mean a small but sufficient amount.

questions.q: We have ___ time, so let's not rush.
questions.why: 'Time' is uncountable here, so use 'a little'.

questions.q: Only ___ students passed the difficult exam.
questions.why: 'Students' is countable, so use 'a few' for a small number.

questions.q: There is ___ point in arguing; nobody will change their mind.
questions.why: 'Little' (without 'a') means almost none and is negative in meaning.

questions.q: ___ people understood the joke, so the room stayed silent.
questions.why: 'Few' (without 'a') means almost none and carries a negative sense.

questions.q: He has ___ of experience for someone so young.
questions.why: After 'a lot' use 'of' before a noun; here 'a lot of experience' is correct, and 'a lot of' stands alone in this slot.

questions.q: She has ___ books on her shelf.
questions.why: 'A lot of' works with both countable and uncountable nouns in affirmative sentences.

questions.q: There are too ___ cars in the parking lot.
questions.why: Use 'too many' with countable nouns to mean an excessive number.

questions.q: You added too ___ salt to the soup.
questions.why: Use 'too much' with uncountable nouns to mean an excessive amount.

questions.q: We don't have ___ chairs for all the guests.
questions.why: 'Enough' means a sufficient quantity and goes before the noun it describes.

questions.q: This coffee isn't sweet ___.
questions.why: 'Enough' comes after an adjective: 'sweet enough'.

questions.q: ___ of the students finished the test on time.
questions.why: Use 'none of' before 'the' plus a noun; 'no' is used directly before a noun without 'of'.

questions.q: There are ___ tickets left for tonight's show.
questions.why: 'No' goes directly before a noun to mean zero.

questions.q: 'How many eggs are there?' 'There are ___.'
questions.why: 'None' stands alone without a following noun as a pronoun.

questions.q: I'd like ___ information about your courses, please.
questions.why: 'Information' is uncountable, so use 'some' (not 'a few' or 'many').

questions.q: There weren't ___ seats available on the late train.
questions.why: Use 'many' with countable 'seats' in a negative sentence.

questions.q: If you have ___ questions, feel free to ask after class.
questions.why: Use 'any' in conditional 'if' clauses with plural countable nouns.

questions.q: Type much or many: 'How ___ sugar do you take in your tea?'
questions.why: 'Sugar' is uncountable, so use 'much'.

questions.q: Type 'a few' or 'a little': 'I need ___ help with this exercise.'
questions.why: 'Help' is uncountable, so use 'a little' for a small amount.

questions.q: Type some or any: 'She didn't make ___ mistakes on the test.'
questions.why: Use 'any' in negative sentences.

questions.q: Type 'few' or 'little': 'He has very ___ patience, so don't keep him waiting.'
questions.why: 'Patience' is uncountable, and 'very little' means almost none.
